extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, patent practitioners, USPTO examiners, and policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and catalog of doctrinal standards and administrative guidance relevant to determining patentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and the USPTO's practices for issuing and organizing such guidance. Focuses on case law tests, policy rationales, and agency guidance forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-ineligible categories (Diamond v. Diehr)
rubrics_metrics.description: Three categories—'laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas'—are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Diamond v. Diehr (450 U.S. 175, 185 (1981)) and examples noted in the text (e.g., a new mineral discovered in the earth or a new plant found in the wild is not patentable; Einstein could not patent E=mc2; Newton could not patent the law of gravity). Use these categories as the baseline exclusion for § 101 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machine-or-transformation test (as a clue)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed process is patent-eligible under § 101 if (1) it is tied to a particular machine or apparatus, or (2) it transforms a particular article into a different state or thing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Supreme Court rejected this as the exclusive test (Bilski) but noted it could nonetheless be an 'important clue.' Use as an indicium rather than a dispositive rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo/Alice two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: First, determine whether the claims at issue are directed at one of the patent-ineligible concepts (laws of nature, natural phenomena, abstract ideas). Second, search for an 'inventive concept' by evaluating the elements of each claim both individually and 'as an ordered combination' to determine whether the additional elements 'transform the nature of the claim' into a patent-eligible application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This two-step inquiry (articulated in Mayo and Alice) is the operative test in much recent case law, though commentators describe it as lacking coherence and often subjective. Apply step 1 to identify ineligible concepts and step 2 to find whether the claim adds an inventive concept beyond that ineligible concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider claims as a whole (Diehr holistic principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims must be considered as a whole; it is inappropriate to dissect the claims into old and new elements and then ignore the presence of the old elements in the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diamond v. Diehr directs holistic consideration of claims. The draft legislative text and some USPTO guidance emphasize holistic eligibility determinations, which tend to favor patentability because otherwise-ineligible elements may be rendered eligible when considered alongside other claim limitations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory approach to patentability (§ 101 should be limited)
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the statutory requirements of patentability—explicit § 101 categories, utility, novelty (§ 102), obviousness (§ 103), and specification (§ 112)—to resolve controversial patentability questions instead of broad judicial exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advocated as a 'scalpel' alternative to judicially created doctrines (the 'machete'). Proponents argue strict application of statutory sections can satisfactorily address questions like business-method patents; the draft bill's removal of the word 'new' before 'useful' also reaffirms that 'newness' is handled by § 102.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural justification for § 101 (early disposition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat subject-matter eligibility as a predominantly legal question that can be decided at the threshold, allowing dismissal of suits on § 101 grounds at the motion-to-dismiss or judgment-on-the-pleadings stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This procedural use of § 101 is defended because it provides a means to quickly and cheaply dispose of infringement claims that obviously lack merit. Recent case law (e.g., Berkheimer, Aatrix) complicates this where factual issues exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual-question caveat (Berkheimer/Aatrix impact)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility determinations may sometimes involve factual questions that preclude resolution on a motion to dismiss or summary judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Berkheimer v. HP and Aatrix Software found factual questions can preclude early dismissal; however, some legislative proposals and USPTO guidance seek to remove or minimize such factual inquiries from § 101 analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Draft legislative reform features affecting eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft bill provisions include deleting 'new' before 'useful', codifying holistic eligibility, creating a presumption in favor of eligibility, abrogating judicial exceptions, and removing Berkheimer-type factual elements from § 101 analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collectively these changes would skew toward expanding eligibility (making more subject matter patentable) but also include adjustments (e.g., § 112 changes) that could constrain claim breadth. Use these features to assess proposed statutory impacts on eligibility determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy rationales for maintaining eligibility hurdles
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility doctrine can serve policy aims: (a) preventing patents on general ideas that impede follow-on innovation; (b) keeping basic science in the public domain; (c) acting as an 'overclaiming test' to clarify patent scope and leave room for improvement; (d) excluding inventions 'socially inappropriate' to patent from a welfare perspective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different commentators emphasize different rationales. When evaluating or crafting eligibility doctrine, consider these policy goals and their trade-offs (e.g., innovation incentives vs. access to foundational knowledge).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'guidance' (agency practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Guidance' encompasses virtually any agency statement that is applicable to a general class of persons but does not rise to the status of a legislative rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance can take the form of orders, notices, memoranda, manuals, FAQs, letters, slides, training materials, and other statements. Recognize this broad scope when assessing USPTO materials and their legal weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: MPEP § 2106 as a primary compilation
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP § 2106 provides a flowchart, descriptions, examples, and interpretations of case law related to subject-matter eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP serves largely an archival function; more recent memos (e.g., Berkheimer memo, 2019 guidance) may supersede MPEP language and later be incorporated in revisions. Use MPEP as a baseline reference but check for superseding USPTO memos and Federal Register notices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types and organization of USPTO guidance materials
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO publishes many forms of guidance on an SME (subject matter eligibility) webpage under headers like 'examination guidance,' 'examples,' 'other materials,' and 'how to comment.' Materials include memos to examiners, training materials, examples, FAQs, slides, transcripts, and indices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The SME website contains a large, sometimes disorganized, set of documents (dozens of items, many files per item). Practitioners should expect memos to be accompanied by examples and training units and should search multiple subpages/archives to locate all relevant materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal Register publication and public-comment mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO guidance may be published in the Federal Register in various forms: requests for written comments, extensions of comment periods, public roundtables/forums, and final guidance documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all USPTO guidance appears in the Federal Register; the Federal Register record is narrower than the SME website. When evaluating the force or outreach of guidance, note whether it was put in the Federal Register (and solicited comment) versus posted solely on the USPTO site.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accompanying examples and training as part of guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Virtually every PTO memo or guidance is accompanied by examples and often forms part of a training unit (audio, PowerPoint, worksheets with answer keys).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples are integral to how guidance is operationalized for examiners; use examples and training materials to interpret how the USPTO expects examiners to apply case law and policy in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Search and keyword heuristics for identifying § 101 guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Relevant searches for USPTO/Federal Register materials should include terms like '35 U.S.C. 101', 'Sec. 101', 'subject matter eligibility', and 'statutory subject matter'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author found certain documents dropped out if keywords differed; comprehensive searches should use multiple common variants to capture relevant guidance and notices.
